items.prompt: Priya sent one accurate, pixel-perfect Figma frame showing the checkout screen's default state. Why did the shipped screen still drift from her intent?
choices: The frame wasn't accurate enough for the default state it showed
A file only shows the state someone drew — it wasn't a spec covering every state, value, and edge case an engineer needs
Engineers always ignore Figma files regardless of what's in them
The frame should have been sent as a PDF instead of a Figma link
items.explanation: A design file is a snapshot of what one state looks like when everything goes right. Being accurate about that one state doesn't make it a spec — a spec has to cover every state, exact values, and edge cases, which a single frame structurally can't carry unless someone deliberately adds that information.
items.reference:
File

What one state looks like

Spec

What to build for every state

Why: a file's accuracy about one state says nothing about its completeness across all states.

items.prompt: A designer says 'the file is ready, every pixel is exactly right.' What question does that claim leave unanswered?
choices: Whether the colors used are on-brand
Whether every state, edge case, and exact value an engineer needs was actually included, not just the one state shown
Whether the file was exported at the right resolution
Whether the designer used the correct font
items.explanation: Pixel accuracy in the state that's shown says nothing about coverage of the states that aren't shown. 'Ready' has to mean complete across situations, not just correct in the one situation someone happened to draw.
items.reference:
File

What one state looks like

Spec

What to build for every state

Why: a file's accuracy about one state says nothing about its completeness across all states.

items.prompt: What's the core difference between a 'design file' and a 'spec,' as used in this unit?
choices: A spec is just a file exported to PDF
A file shows what a state looks like; a spec tells an engineer what to build across every state, value, and edge case
There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
A spec is written by engineers, a file is written by designers
items.explanation: A file is a visual snapshot. A spec is an instruction set — it has to cover situations the file doesn't show, name exact values instead of leaving them to be measured, and make clear what's load-bearing.
items.reference:
File

What one state looks like

Spec

What to build for every state

Why: a file's accuracy about one state says nothing about its completeness across all states.

items.prompt: Sam shipped a static checkmark instead of the animated success state Priya intended. What does this unit say actually caused that gap?
choices: Sam was careless and didn't look closely enough at the design
Sam filled a genuine gap in the handoff with a reasonable guess, because no durable reference for the animation existed
Engineers are generally uninterested in visual polish
The Figma file was corrupted when Sam opened it
items.explanation: Reinterpretation isn't usually carelessness — it's an engineer filling a real gap the only way they can, with a guess made under a deadline using whatever's actually visible or remembered.
items.reference:
A gap in the handoff + a deadline = a reasonable guess, not a careless mistake.

Why: blaming the engineer's care level misses that the guess was the only option a gap in the handoff left available.

items.prompt: Why does this unit avoid framing shipped drift as 'the engineer didn't care enough'?
choices: Because engineers are never at fault for anything
Because the drift traces back to a genuine gap in what the handoff carried, which a guess fills whether or not the engineer is careful
Because designers are always more careful than engineers
Because blame doesn't matter as long as the bug gets fixed eventually
items.explanation: Framing it as a care problem misdiagnoses the failure and points the fix at the wrong thing (try harder) instead of the actual fix (carry more information in the handoff itself).
items.reference:
A gap in the handoff + a deadline = a reasonable guess, not a careless mistake.

Why: blaming the engineer's care level misses that the guess was the only option a gap in the handoff left available.

items.prompt: Priya's checkout screen had five real states: default, loading, success, error, and empty. Why does listing 'default' alone leave the biggest gaps?
choices: Default is actually the hardest state to build correctly
Every state besides default is what happens when things DON'T go as planned — exactly the situations an engineer can't infer from a single happy-path screenshot
Loading and error states never actually occur in real products
Engineers prefer building the default state first regardless of what's specified
items.explanation: The default/happy-path state is the one an engineer can usually infer correctly from a screenshot. Every other state exists specifically to handle something going differently than planned — which is exactly what a single frame can't show unless someone draws it.
items.reference:
✅ Default — shown, easy to infer
❌ Loading, empty, error, success — not shown, must be drawn or guessed

Why: the states most likely to be missed are exactly the ones a happy-path screenshot can't reveal.

items.prompt: An engineer asks 'what happens if the cart is empty at checkout?' and there's no answer in the handoff. What should this question tell the team?
choices: That the engineer is overthinking an unlikely edge case
That a real state exists that was never specified, and someone will guess unless it gets designed
That the checkout flow should be scrapped and redesigned
That empty carts should be technically impossible so the question doesn't matter
items.explanation: A question with no answer in the handoff is a signal that a real state slipped through, not a sign the engineer is being difficult. The alternative to answering it isn't 'the situation won't happen' — it's 'someone will guess.'
items.reference:
✅ Default — shown, easy to infer
❌ Loading, empty, error, success — not shown, must be drawn or guessed

Why: the states most likely to be missed are exactly the ones a happy-path screenshot can't reveal.

items.prompt: Which of these is most likely to be silently missing from a handoff that only shows one screenshot?
choices: The main button's label text
The empty state, shown when there's nothing to display
The screen's primary background color
The page title
items.explanation: A single screenshot almost always shows a populated, successful state — the empty state is, by definition, the one situation that screenshot structurally cannot depict.
items.reference:
✅ Default — shown, easy to infer
❌ Loading, empty, error, success — not shown, must be drawn or guessed

Why: the states most likely to be missed are exactly the ones a happy-path screenshot can't reveal.

items.prompt: Which handoff artifact is specifically meant to prevent an engineer from having to measure spacing by eye?
choices: A higher-resolution export of the design file
A named design token, like spacing-lg = 24px
A longer Slack message describing the screen
A second screenshot of the same state
items.explanation: A design token is a named, documented value an engineer reads instead of measures — removing the step where a pixel value gets estimated off a screenshot or a layer's incidental structure.
items.reference:
Token = a named value, read not measured. Annotation = a note attached to the file explaining a rule or reason.

Why: different artifacts close different gaps — a token closes a measurement gap specifically.

items.prompt: What's the main purpose of an annotation on a handoff file (a note about spacing, sizing, or interaction attached to the design)?
choices: To make the file look more professional
To carry the exact rule or reason a value was chosen, instead of leaving it to be inferred from the visual alone
To replace the need for any conversation between design and engineering
To satisfy a company style guide requirement
items.explanation: An annotation exists to make an otherwise-invisible rule visible and durable — the reason behind a spacing choice, or a rule that applies but isn't obvious just from looking at the shape on screen.
items.reference:
Token = a named value, read not measured. Annotation = a note attached to the file explaining a rule or reason.

Why: different artifacts close different gaps — a token closes a measurement gap specifically.

items.prompt: What does design QA check that a normal engineering code review can't?
choices: Whether the code follows the team's style guide
Whether what actually got built matches the designer's original intent, not just whether the code works correctly
Whether the code has any security vulnerabilities
Whether the code passes its automated test suite
items.explanation: Code review checks whether code is correct and maintainable — it doesn't check whether the built screen matches what the designer intended, because the reviewer usually can't see the original design intent, only the code.
items.reference:
Code review asks: does this code work? Design QA asks: does this screen match the intent?

Why: the two checks answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

items.prompt: A team ships a feature that passes all engineering code review and every automated test. Does that mean the shipped screen matches the design?
choices: Yes — passing review and tests is proof the design was followed exactly
Not necessarily — code review and tests check that the code works, not that it matches the designer's original intent
Only if the tests specifically mention the design file
Yes, but only for the default state
items.explanation: Code review and automated tests verify the code works as written — they have no way of checking whether what was written matches an intent that lives in a design file they don't reference.
items.reference:
Code review asks: does this code work? Design QA asks: does this screen match the intent?

Why: the two checks answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

items.prompt: Why is design QA a distinct step from engineering code review, rather than something code review can just absorb?
choices: Because reviewers don't have access to the codebase
Because matching intent requires comparing the build to the original design, which is a different check than verifying the code itself works
Because design QA is only needed for mobile apps
Because code review happens after launch, not before
items.explanation: The two checks require different reference points — code review compares code to itself (does it work, is it maintainable); design QA compares the rendered result to the design intent, which lives outside the codebase entirely.
items.reference:
Code review asks: does this code work? Design QA asks: does this screen match the intent?

Why: the two checks answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

items.prompt: In the handoff loop described in this unit, where does design QA sit relative to the build?
choices: Strictly after launch, as a retrospective exercise
Early enough, during the build, that a found gap can route back into work still in progress
Before the spec is even written
It replaces the spec entirely, so no spec is needed if QA happens
items.explanation: The loop only works if design QA happens while the build is still open — a gap found mid-build routes back as an in-progress fix; a gap found after merge and scheduling requires reopening finished work.
items.reference:
Spec → Build → QA (mid-build) → fixes route back into Build, or → Ship if it matches.

Why: QA's value depends entirely on timing — the same check, done late, has nowhere cheap to route a fix.

items.prompt: Why does this unit describe the handoff process as a loop rather than a straight line from design to launch?
choices: Because designs always need to be redone from scratch after QA
Because design QA is meant to feed findings back into an in-progress build, not just confirm or deny a finished one
Because engineers and designers work in completely separate loops that never connect
Because loops are a more visually interesting diagram shape
items.explanation: A straight line implies QA is a final yes/no gate. A loop reflects that QA's real purpose is catching drift while there's still an open place to route the fix — back into the same build, not into a separate post-launch effort.
items.reference:
Spec → Build → QA (mid-build) → fixes route back into Build, or → Ship if it matches.

Why: QA's value depends entirely on timing — the same check, done late, has nowhere cheap to route a fix.

items.prompt: A team schedules design QA for the day before launch, after the code is merged and the release is scheduled. What does the loop diagram in this unit suggest about that timing?
choices: It's fine, because QA's job is only to confirm the release is ready
It breaks the loop — a gap found then has nowhere cheap to route back to, since the build is already closed out
It's actually the ideal timing, since it catches issues closest to what will actually ship
Timing doesn't affect the cost of whatever QA finds
items.explanation: QA still finds the same gaps either way, but late timing removes the cheap path back into an open build — a found gap now means reopening merged, reviewed, scheduled work instead of adjusting something still in progress.
items.reference:
Spec → Build → QA (mid-build) → fixes route back into Build, or → Ship if it matches.

Why: QA's value depends entirely on timing — the same check, done late, has nowhere cheap to route a fix.

items.prompt: Sam read spacing off Figma's inspector and got 16px instead of Priya's intended 24px. Why does a design token prevent this specific failure, where the inspector didn't?
choices: Because tokens are always more precise numbers than pixel values
Because a token is a named, documented value read directly, while the inspector reports what a specific layer's structure happens to compute — which can differ from the intended rule
Because Figma's inspector is buggy and shouldn't be trusted for any value
Because tokens eliminate the need for spacing to be consistent at all
items.explanation: The inspector measures the accident of one layer's structure, not the designer's intended rule. A token is the rule itself, documented and named — reading it can't produce a different number than what was intended, because there's no measurement step to introduce drift.
items.reference:
Eyeball/inspectorMeasures this layer's accident
TokenReads the documented, intended rule

Why: measurement drifts; reading a named value can't.

items.prompt: Beyond fixing one spacing bug, what's the broader benefit of using design tokens across a whole product?
choices: It makes the Figma file load faster
A hundred instances of the same intended value share one true source instead of each being independently measured and independently able to drift
It removes the need for engineers to look at Figma at all
It guarantees the product will never need a redesign
items.explanation: Without tokens, every instance of 'the same' spacing value is really an independent measurement, each capable of drifting differently. A shared token means one true value backs every instance, so they can't quietly diverge from each other.
items.reference:
Eyeball/inspectorMeasures this layer's accident
TokenReads the documented, intended rule

Why: measurement drifts; reading a named value can't.

items.prompt: What does an annotation add that the visual layout of a design frame doesn't already communicate on its own?
choices: Nothing — a good enough visual always communicates everything an engineer needs
The reasoning or exact rule behind a choice, which isn't visible just from looking at the resulting shape
The file's export settings
A record of which designer worked on the file
items.explanation: A visual shows the result of a decision, not the decision's reasoning or its exact, checkable rule. An annotation makes that invisible layer — why, and exactly how much — available to whoever builds it.
items.reference:
A shape on screen shows a result. It doesn't show the rule behind it or whether that rule is load-bearing elsewhere.

Why: annotations exist specifically to carry what a visual structurally cannot.

items.prompt: Priya's 24px spacing matched a token used on the two screens before checkout, for visual continuity across the flow. If that reasoning had been annotated on the frame, what specifically would it have prevented?
choices: Nothing — annotations don't affect what gets built
It would have flagged the spacing as load-bearing (tied to continuity across screens) rather than a value an engineer could reasonably treat as approximate
It would have made the checkout flow load faster
It would have prevented Sam from working on the project at all
items.explanation: Without the annotation, 16px vs 24px looks like an inconsequential rounding difference. With it, the value is explicitly tied to a cross-screen consistency goal — marking it as something to get exactly right, not eyeball.
items.reference:
A shape on screen shows a result. It doesn't show the rule behind it or whether that rule is load-bearing elsewhere.

Why: annotations exist specifically to carry what a visual structurally cannot.

items.prompt: Which situation most needs an annotation, rather than relying on the visual alone?
choices: A button whose color is obviously the brand's primary color, visible in the frame
A spacing value that's identical to a value used elsewhere in the product, for a specific consistency reason
Text that's already legible and correctly spelled in the frame
An icon that's already a standard, recognizable icon
items.explanation: The self-evident cases (obvious brand color, legible text, standard icon) don't need extra explanation — the visual already carries the needed information. A value whose exact match to another screen matters for a reason invisible in the frame is exactly the case an annotation is for.
items.reference:
A shape on screen shows a result. It doesn't show the rule behind it or whether that rule is load-bearing elsewhere.

Why: annotations exist specifically to carry what a visual structurally cannot.

items.prompt: Which pair of states is most commonly missing from a design handoff, according to this unit's checklist?
choices: Default and loading
Empty and error
Hover and focus
Light mode and dark mode
items.explanation: Empty and error states describe what happens when something isn't going as planned — exactly the situations a single, successful-looking screenshot doesn't reveal and is easiest to forget to design at all.
items.reference:
Checklist: all states, tokens not pixels, motion notes, copy per state, a scheduled QA pass.

Why: a checklist is checkable by someone other than the person who wrote it — 'ready' is a feeling, a checklist item is a fact.

items.prompt: Why does this unit prefer a checklist over a designer simply feeling confident the handoff is 'ready'?
choices: Because designers can't be trusted to judge their own work
Because a checklist is checkable by someone else, while a feeling of readiness isn't verifiable and can be wrong without anyone noticing
Because checklists are required by most design tools
Because feelings of readiness are always wrong
items.explanation: 'Ready' as a feeling can't be independently verified — Priya genuinely felt her file was ready. A checklist turns that feeling into discrete, checkable items someone else (an engineer, a design QA reviewer) can confirm or flag as missing.
items.reference:
Checklist: all states, tokens not pixels, motion notes, copy per state, a scheduled QA pass.

Why: a checklist is checkable by someone other than the person who wrote it — 'ready' is a feeling, a checklist item is a fact.

items.prompt: What determines whether a handoff is complete, according to the model in this unit?
choices: Whether the file looks visually finished and polished
Whether an engineer could build every state correctly without needing to ask a follow-up question
Whether the file was reviewed by a design lead
Whether the file contains at least ten screens
items.explanation: 'Looks finished' and 'is complete' are different properties — a polished single screenshot can still leave every other state undefined. Completeness is measured by whether the gaps that would force a guess have actually been closed.
items.reference:
Complete = no follow-up question needed. Polished = looks finished. The two aren't the same.

Why: a handoff can look done and still leave real gaps unclosed.

items.prompt: A designer spends extra time polishing visual details in a frame that already shows the default state clearly. What does this unit imply about whether that time closes the handoff's real gaps?
choices: It always closes the gaps, since more polish is always better
Not necessarily — polishing what's already clear doesn't address the states, values, or reasoning that are missing entirely
It closes the gaps only if the polish involves color changes
Polish time and completeness are unrelated to each other in every case
items.explanation: Time spent making an already-clear state more polished doesn't address what's actually missing — the states, exact values, and reasoning that were never included at all. Completeness and polish are different axes.
items.reference:
Complete = no follow-up question needed. Polished = looks finished. The two aren't the same.

Why: a handoff can look done and still leave real gaps unclosed.

items.prompt: Which handoff is more complete: one with four polished screenshots of the default state, or one with five rough sketches covering default, loading, empty, error, and success?
choices: The four polished screenshots, since polish signals quality
The five rough sketches, since completeness is about covering every state an engineer needs, not visual polish
They're equally complete since both took similar effort
Neither — completeness requires at least ten screens regardless of content
items.explanation: Coverage of the states an engineer actually needs to build matters more than visual fidelity of the states already shown. Five rough but complete sketches leave fewer gaps for guessing than four polished but incomplete ones.
items.reference:
Complete = no follow-up question needed. Polished = looks finished. The two aren't the same.

Why: a handoff can look done and still leave real gaps unclosed.

items.prompt: Of the five gaps in the checkout incident, four resulted in a shipped guess and one shipped correctly. What was different about the one that shipped correctly?
choices: It was the simplest state to build technically
It was the one state the handoff artifact actually specified — the only one with a durable, checkable reference
Sam happened to spend more time on that particular state
It was the last state Sam worked on, so he had more context by then
items.explanation: The loading state shipped correctly because it was the one state the single frame actually showed. The pattern across all five gaps is that presence of a durable reference — not effort, skill, or ordering — determined the outcome.
items.reference:
4 of 5 states were unspecified and required a guess. The 1 correct state was the 1 specified state.

Why: the incident's pattern is about presence of a reference, not engineer effort or skill.

items.prompt: The error state was attempted by Sam using a color he found in an old file, but it was still wrong. What does this specific gap illustrate that the totally-missing empty state doesn't?
choices: That partial effort is always worse than no effort at all
That having *some* reference (an old file) still isn't the same as having the actual intended reference (a documented token) — proximity to a source doesn't guarantee it's the right one
That error states are inherently harder to build than empty states
That Sam should have asked more questions in general
items.explanation: The error-state gap shows a subtler failure mode than 'nothing existed to reference' — something plausible-looking existed (an old file's color), and using it still produced the wrong value, because it wasn't the actual documented, intended token.
items.reference:
4 of 5 states were unspecified and required a guess. The 1 correct state was the 1 specified state.

Why: the incident's pattern is about presence of a reference, not engineer effort or skill.

items.prompt: What's the single pattern that explains all five gaps in the checkout incident, according to the L3 trace?
choices: Sam consistently made poor technical decisions
Wherever a durable, checkable reference existed, the build matched it; wherever it didn't, a guess filled the gap
Priya's designs were fundamentally too complex to implement
The team simply needed a longer development timeline
items.explanation: Across all five gaps, the outcome tracked one variable: whether a durable reference existed. It didn't track effort, skill, or how much time was available — reinforcing that the fix is closing reference gaps, not adding more time or trying harder.
items.reference:
4 of 5 states were unspecified and required a guess. The 1 correct state was the 1 specified state.

Why: the incident's pattern is about presence of a reference, not engineer effort or skill.

items.prompt: Design QA on day 28 found the same number of gaps it likely would have found on day 5. What actually got worse from the delay, according to the incident trace?
choices: Nothing — the delay had no real consequence since the same gaps were found either way
The cost and category of the fix — a value swap versus new logic retrofitted under a rushed deadline with less scrutiny
The total number of gaps found increased because of the delay
The delay only affected the empty-cart bug, not the others
items.explanation: Bug count doesn't scale with lateness — the same drift exists whether it's caught early or late. What scales is the cost and risk of fixing it: an adjustment to in-progress work versus reopening merged, reviewed, scheduled code under deadline pressure.
items.reference:
Spacing fix (found late): 20 minutes, low risk. Empty-cart fix (found late): rushed new logic, shipped with a new problem.

Why: lateness changes the category of fix required, not just its cost.

items.prompt: The empty-cart fix that shipped under a two-day deadline was itself wrong — it disabled the button instead of showing Priya's originally designed illustrated state. What does this reveal about rushed, late-stage fixes?
choices: That rushed fixes are always technically inferior code
That a rushed fix made without time to check against the original spec can reproduce the exact same failure — a guess filling a gap — just compressed into a shorter window
That the empty-cart bug was actually impossible to fix correctly
That the fix would have been correct regardless of how much time was available
items.explanation: The rushed fix wasn't a different kind of problem — it was a smaller-scale replay of the original failure: a real decision got made without checking it against what was actually specified, because there wasn't time to check.
items.reference:
Spacing fix (found late): 20 minutes, low risk. Empty-cart fix (found late): rushed new logic, shipped with a new problem.

Why: lateness changes the category of fix required, not just its cost.

items.prompt: Why did the spacing fix take twenty minutes while the empty-cart fix required a rushed one-day patch, even though both were found on the same day?
choices: The spacing bug was found first, giving the team a head start
The spacing fix was a value substitution with no new logic; the empty-cart fix required new logic retrofitted into already-merged, already-reviewed code
The empty-cart bug was simply reported with less clarity
Spacing bugs are inherently always faster to fix than any other bug type
items.explanation: The two fixes differ in kind, not just difficulty: one is a value swap into existing structure, the other is new functionality that has to be designed, written, and shipped without the normal review time a feature would otherwise get.
items.reference:
Spacing fix (found late): 20 minutes, low risk. Empty-cart fix (found late): rushed new logic, shipped with a new problem.

Why: lateness changes the category of fix required, not just its cost.

items.prompt: Sam's 16px spacing came from Figma's inspector reporting the auto-layout's computed gap. Why does this specific detail matter to the diagnosis, rather than just 'he measured wrong'?
choices: It doesn't matter — 'measured wrong' fully explains the bug
It shows the inspector was reporting a real, accurate number — just the number for a different question (this layer's structure) than the one that mattered (the intended token)
It proves Figma's inspector tool is fundamentally broken
It shows Sam never actually looked at the spacing at all
items.explanation: The inspector wasn't lying or malfunctioning — 16px was a real, accurately reported number. The failure is that it answered a different question (what does this layer currently compute) than the one Sam needed answered (what value did the designer intend), and nothing flagged that mismatch.
items.reference:
Inspector reports: what this layer computes right now. Token would report: what value was actually intended.

Why: an accurate answer to the wrong question still produces a wrong outcome.

items.prompt: The 24px spacing mattered because it matched a token used on the two screens before checkout, for continuity across the flow. If checkout had been a standalone screen with no adjacent flow, would the same 16px-vs-24px gap have mattered as much?
choices: Yes, identically — spacing precision always matters the same amount regardless of context

Less — the calibration principle from this unit says a value's importance depends on whether getting it wrong changes something real, like cross-screen consistency, not on the value itself in isolation
No, spacing never matters unless a design token exists for it
It would have mattered more, since standalone screens require more precision
items.explanation: The unit's calibration principle is that a value needs a firm reference specifically when getting it wrong changes something real — here, visual continuity across a flow. Strip out the cross-screen reason and the same numeric gap carries less real consequence, even though it's the same 8px difference.
items.reference:
Inspector reports: what this layer computes right now. Token would report: what value was actually intended.

Why: an accurate answer to the wrong question still produces a wrong outcome.

items.prompt: The success animation gap traces back to something described verbally in a design review three weeks before Sam built it. What does the unit say is the real problem with that as a handoff mechanism?
choices: That design reviews shouldn't happen at all
That it depends entirely on unaided memory surviving weeks of unrelated work, with nothing durable to check against later
That Sam wasn't paying attention during the review
That verbal communication is always inferior to written communication in every context
items.explanation: The specific failure isn't 'verbal is bad' in general — it's that this particular verbal detail had no durable form at all, so its survival depended entirely on memory across a three-week gap with other work in between, which is a fragile mechanism regardless of how attentive anyone was in the moment.
items.reference:
A written spec is unchanged on day 27, exactly as it was on day 0. A verbal detail depends on memory surviving that same gap.

Why: durability, not format, is what a handoff mechanism needs to guarantee.

items.prompt: Why doesn't 'Sam was in the room when it was discussed' close the handoff gap the way a written note would?
choices: It does close the gap completely — being present is sufficient
Being present captures the information once, in the moment, but a handoff needs the information to still be accurate and checkable weeks later when it's actually needed
Sam wasn't actually paying attention during the meeting
Verbal information is technically impossible to remember at all
items.explanation: Presence solves 'did the information reach someone,' but a handoff also needs 'will it still be there, accurately, when it's needed' — and unaided memory across weeks of unrelated work is a much weaker guarantee of that than a document that hasn't changed.
items.reference:
A written spec is unchanged on day 27, exactly as it was on day 0. A verbal detail depends on memory surviving that same gap.

Why: durability, not format, is what a handoff mechanism needs to guarantee.

items.prompt: What's the general lesson from the success-animation gap, beyond this specific incident?
choices: Animations should never be used in product design
Any detail communicated only once, verbally, with no durable record, is at risk regardless of how important it felt in the moment or how attentive the listener was
Design reviews should be eliminated to prevent this kind of gap
Only senior engineers can be trusted to remember verbal details
items.explanation: The transferable lesson isn't about animations specifically — it's that anything that only exists as a spoken detail in a meeting is vulnerable to being forgotten or deprioritized later, no matter how clearly it was communicated at the time.
items.reference:
A written spec is unchanged on day 27, exactly as it was on day 0. A verbal detail depends on memory surviving that same gap.

Why: durability, not format, is what a handoff mechanism needs to guarantee.

items.prompt: This unit warns against documenting every internal wrapper's padding and annotating decisions with no real ambiguity. What question does it offer instead, to decide what actually needs a token or annotation?
choices: "Would this look impressive in a design review?"
"Is there a real decision here an engineer could reasonably make differently than I intend?"
"Has this value been documented anywhere before?"
"Would documenting this take less than five minutes?"
items.explanation: The calibration test isn't about exhaustiveness or effort — it's about whether skipping the annotation leaves room for a genuinely different, reasonable interpretation. Values with only one obvious reading don't need it; values with real ambiguity do.
items.reference:
Needs a token/annotationRepeats across screens; wrong reading changes behavior; nobody would think to ask
Doesn'tLocal, one-off, self-evident from the visual

Why: over-speccing has its own real cost — a document nobody reads closely.

items.prompt: What does this unit say is the actual cost of over-specifying a handoff (documenting every trivial, unambiguous detail)?
choices: There is no real cost — more documentation is always strictly better
It costs real designer time and produces a document dense enough that engineers stop reading it closely, burying the details that actually mattered
It only costs money, never time or attention
It makes the design file too large to open
items.explanation: Over-specification isn't free just because it's well-intentioned — the real cost is that a document too dense to skim buries the few genuinely load-bearing details among many that didn't need stating, making the important ones easier to miss, not harder.
items.reference:
Needs a token/annotationRepeats across screens; wrong reading changes behavior; nobody would think to ask
Doesn'tLocal, one-off, self-evident from the visual

Why: over-speccing has its own real cost — a document nobody reads closely.

items.prompt: A tooltip's padding is a one-off value nobody is likely to scrutinize, and it's self-evident from the visual. Should it get a dedicated design token, according to this unit's calibration guidance?
